questions.question: In a market with privately informed sellers whose quality matters to buyers, what does the word \"adverse\" in adverse selection refer to?
options: Those who accept are disproportionately the types worst for the offer-maker
The informed side deliberately lies about its type to the uninformed side
The uninformed side selects the worst types on purpose to pay less
Prices are always set below every type's value, which is adverse for sellers

questions.question: A buyer offers price $p$ to a seller whose quality is $L$ or $H$, private to the seller; low types accept lower prices. When computing her expected value of the good at a price that only $L$ types accept, which expectation should she use?
options: The unconditional mean value over both quality levels
The mean value conditional on the good being of quality $L$
The value of an $H$ good, since that is what she hopes to buy
The average of the two seller values for $L$ and $H$

questions.question: An insurer covers a population in which 60% are low-risk customers with expected loss 20 and 40% are high-risk customers with expected loss 60. If everyone buys at one pooled premium, which premium makes the insurer break even?

An insurer charges one premium of 36 to a population of 60% low-risk (expected loss 20) and 40% high-risk (expected loss 60) customers. Low-risk customers will pay at most 25 and drop out. What is the expected claim per remaining customer?

Sellers privately know whether their good is high or low quality, and a buyer chooses between a high price that every type accepts and a low price that only low types accept. Why does a larger share of high-quality sellers make the high price more attractive?
options: It lowers the price the high-quality sellers are willing to accept
It makes the low price unacceptable to the low-quality sellers
It lets the buyer identify the quality before she makes her offer
It raises the buyer's expected value among the sellers who accept

questions.question: A buyer makes a take-it-or-leave-it price offer to a seller whose quality type $\theta\in\{L,H\}$ is private. In the Bayesian Nash equilibrium of this game, what is the seller's strategy?
options: A rule giving, for each type, whether to accept each possible price
A single decision to accept or reject, chosen before learning her type
The price she would ask if she could make the offer herself
Her expected value of the good, averaged over both types

questions.question: A seller privately knows if her good is of high quality $H$ (probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$) or low quality $L$; she values $H$ at 8 and $L$ at 2, a buyer values them at 11 and 3. The buyer offers a price $p$; each seller type accepts iff $p$ is at least her own value. A buyer reasons: \"the average good is worth 7 to me, so offering 6 gives me $7-6=1$.\" What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: At $p=6$ only $L$ sellers accept, so the relevant value is 3
She should compare 7 with the average seller value 5
The average must weight $H$ more heavily since it is worth more
At $p=6$ only $H$ sellers accept, so the value is 11

questions.question: A seller's type $t$ is uniform on $[0,1]$; she values her good at $t$ and the buyer at $1.5t$, so every trade has gains. The buyer offers $p\in(0,1]$, accepted iff $t\le p$. What is the buyer's expected value of the good conditional on acceptance?
options: $\tfrac{p}{2}$

questions.question: An insurer sees 70% low-risk customers (expected loss 10, willing to pay up to 18) and 30% high-risk customers (expected loss 40, willing to pay up to 50). It can charge only one premium and must break even. What happens?
options: Both groups are insured at 19, below the high-risk limit of 50
Pooling needs 19 > 18, so only high risks insure, paying at least 40
Both groups are insured at 25, the average of the two expected losses
Only low risks are insured, at 10, since they are the majority
